chunks: I am faced with men who do not obey when I order and do not respond when I call them,
May you have no father! (Woe to you!) What are you waiting for to rise for the cause of Allah?
Does not faith join you together, or sense of shame rouse you?!
I stand among you shouting and I am calling you for help,
but you do not listen to my word, and do not obey my orders,
till circumstance show out their bad consequences.
No blood can be avenged through you and no purpose can be achieved with you.
I called you for help of your brethren but made noises like the camel having pain in stomach,
and became loose like the camel of thin back.
Then a wavering weak contingent came to me from amongst you: “as if they are being led to death and they are only watching.”

key_terms.تَثَاقُلَ النِّضْوِ الْأَدْبَرِ: the sluggishness of the camel with a thin back
key_terms.جَرْجَرَةَ الْجَمَلِ الْأَسِرِّ: the noise of the camel with stomach pain
key_terms.مُنِيتُ: I am faced with / I am afflicted with
key_terms.يُبْلَغُ بِكُمْ مَرَامٌ: a purpose is achieved with you

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of the Quranic verse quoted in Nahj al-Balagha regarding those led to death?
ai.summary: This passage from Nahj al-Balagha captures Imam Ali’s (AS) frustration with the Khurasanians' delay in joining him for the Battle of Siffin, highlighting the critical Shia theme of timely obedience to the Imam's command. The rhetorical question 'What are you waiting for from your Lord?' underscores the urgency of divine support contingent upon human effort, while the vivid metaphors of the lame camel and the rear camel emphasize their sluggishness. This critique serves as a foundational text for understanding the political and spiritual dynamics of the early Islamic community during the Fitna.
